design_detail: Sponsor's briefing document, not a study: the 145-page background package written by the applicant, Lykos Therapeutics (formerly MAPS Public Benefit Corporation, the subsidiary of the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies that ran the trials), for the members of the FDA Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee before its meeting of 4 June 2024 on the new drug application for midomafetamine (MDMA) capsules with a psychological intervention for PTSD, and published by the FDA among the meeting materials. Its purpose is to make the sponsor's case for approval: efficacy, safety, risk management and benefit-risk. It cites neither published phase 3 report; its figures come from the sponsor's clinical study reports (MAPP1 CSR Amendment, MAPP2 CSR, MPLONG interim CSR), its integrated summary of safety and tables dated April 2024. Printed page numbers ('Page X of 145') equal the PDF pages; 76 pages, including most tables and figures, are images without a text layer. New compared with the published trial reports: (1) an observational long-term follow-up of the phase 3 participants (MPLONG: 142 of 194 enrolled; interim results); (2) pooled phase 3 safety tables (99 on MDMA, 95 on placebo), with event-level resolution times, events on dosing days, potentially clinically significant blood pressure by session and suicidality by C-SSRS; (3) MAPP1 responder rates, nominal P values for the responder analyses, de facto and worst-case sensitivity results, SDS responder rates and pooled subgroup estimates; (4) programme-wide serious adverse events and deaths across 17 studies with 427 people exposed; (5) explicit statements of what the phase 3 programme did not collect (subjective and positive drug effects, post-dose ECGs, post-dose laboratory tests); (6) the open-label extension MAPPUSX, in which placebo participants crossed over to MDMA, and the sponsor's account of the misconduct in the phase 2 study MP-4. It contains no new randomized comparison and no analysis of blinding or expectancy.
can_establish: What the sponsor reported to the FDA advisory committee in June 2024: its clinical-study-report figures for the two phase 3 trials, including figures not in the published reports, its pooled safety data, the interim results of its observational follow-up, what its programme did and did not measure, and its proposed risk management; each figure can be cited as the sponsor's.
cannot_establish: Whether the benefit of MDMA-assisted therapy lasts or is due to MDMA: the follow-up is observational, was joined by about 73% of participants, was entered by MAPP1 participants who knew their allocation, and is reported only as figures, percentages of those assessed and nominal P values; nor whether the safety profile is complete, since subjective and positive effects, post-dose ECGs and post-dose laboratory tests were not collected; and nothing in it is peer-reviewed or independent of the applicant.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (sponsor's document). It reports the two phase 3 trials (MAPP1, 90 dosed; MAPP2, 104), the observational follow-up MPLONG, for which people from the sponsor's PTSD studies were 'strongly encouraged' to enrol at least 6 months after their last session (pp. 19, 67-68), and summaries of 15 other sponsor studies (Table 29, pp. 121-127).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Phase 3 criteria as summarized (pp. 44-46): adults over 48 kg with DSM-5 PTSD of 6 months or more, PCL-5 of 46 or more (MAPP1) or 40 or more (MAPP2) at screening and CAPS-5 of 35 or more or 28 or more at baseline; excluded: likely re-exposure to the index trauma or another significant trauma, lack of social support or of a stable living situation, serious suicide risk (defined by recent behaviour and C-SSRS scores), ecstasy use more than 10 times in 10 years or at least once within 6 months of the first session, ketamine within 12 weeks, severe (or moderate, not in early remission) alcohol or cannabis use disorder, other substance use disorders within 12 months, psychotic and bipolar I disorders, dissociative identity disorder, personality disorders, significant cardiovascular or cerebrovascular disease and arrhythmia, symptomatic liver disease, and a history of hyponatraemia or hyperthermia; well-controlled hypertension, asymptomatic hepatitis C, type 2 diabetes, hypothyroidism and glaucoma were allowed. MPLONG: at least one medication session in a sponsor study and agreement to be contacted about 6 months after it (p. 68).
sample.demographics: MPLONG enrollees, MDMA vs placebo (Tables 16 and 17, pp. 70-72): mean age 41.4 vs 39.4; male 32 (42.7%) vs 17 (25.4%); Hispanic or Latino 18 (24.0%) vs 9 (13.4%); White 54 (72.0%) vs 42 (62.7%); veterans 14 (18.7%) vs 11 (16.4%); prior sertraline 25 (33.3%) vs 11 (16.4%); parent-study baseline CAPS-5 40.3 (6.05) vs 40.9 (6.70) and termination CAPS-5 15.9 (12.55) vs 24.9 (12.31); time from the parent study to the follow-up visit mean 15.9 vs 15.8 months, median 12.7 (range 6.1 to 32.7) vs 12.7 (6.0 to 32.9).
sample.attrition: MPLONG: 60 of 90 MAPP1 participants (67%; 30 on MDMA, 30 on placebo) and 82 of 104 MAPP2 participants (79%; 45 and 37) enrolled; 16 and 14 (MAPP1) and 8 and 14 (MAPP2) declined or were lost; 6 of 75 on MDMA and 1 of 67 on placebo discontinued; the effectiveness subset (a follow-up CAPS-5) was 71 and 66, that is 72% and 69% of the 99 and 95 in the phase 3 safety set (editors' calculation) (pp. 22, 68-69). Phase 3 pool: completed 94 (94.9%) vs 80 (84.2%) (Table 18, p. 77).
sample.selection_effects: Enrolment in the follow-up was voluntary and differed by arm and trial (MAPP2 placebo 37 of 51, MDMA 45 of 53); MAPP1 enrollees knew their allocation, since MPLONG opened only after MAPP1's database lock and unblinding (p. 67); 32 of MAPP1's placebo participants later received open-label MDMA in the extension study MAPPUSX (p. 121), and the document does not say whether their follow-up visit came before or after; treatments between the trial and the follow-up visit (psychotherapy, medicines, illicit MDMA use) were collected but are not reported (p. 68).

exposure.measurement: The manualized MDMA-assisted therapy of the phase 3 trials: three 90-minute preparatory sessions, three 8-hour medication sessions with MDMA or inactive placebo, each followed by three 90-minute integration sessions, with sessions rated for adherence on a 20-item checklist (pp. 19, 43-44, 128-130). MPLONG gave no drug or therapy (p. 67).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as reported: by mouth, a split dose per medication session, 80 mg followed by 40 mg in session 1 and 120 mg followed by 60 mg in sessions 2 and 3 (MDMA hydrochloride), the second part 1.5 to 2 hours after the first, sessions 3 to 5 weeks apart; the increase after session 1 was the default but optional; the proposed product is a capsule of 40 or 60 mg MDMA hydrochloride given as three capsules per session, at least 21 days apart (pp. 16, 28, 40-42, Table 3). In the pooled phase 3 set 99 received session 1, 96 session 2 (94 at the higher first part) and 95 session 3 (92) (Table 19, p. 78).
exposure.polysubstance: Psychiatric medicines, including SSRIs and SNRIs, and cannabis were prohibited and tapered before baseline; stimulants for ADHD could continue with pauses around each session; mild, or moderate in early remission, alcohol or cannabis use disorders were allowed (pp. 18, 45, 128).

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo with identical therapy in both phase 3 trials, chosen with the FDA; an active placebo (low-dose MDMA with therapy) and niacin were considered, discussed with the FDA and ruled out as unable to address functional unblinding and/or because a potential anti-therapeutic effect could advantage the active arm (p. 42). MPLONG compares the parent trials' arms as randomized, with no further control.
comparison.matching: Randomization in the parent trials only; among MPLONG enrollees the arms differ in sex (male 42.7% vs 25.4%) and prior sertraline (33.3% vs 16.4%) (Tables 16 and 17).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; for MPLONG, the characteristics of those who did not enrol and the treatments received after the trial are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same eligibility in both arms of the parent trials.

outcomes.instruments: Phase 3: CAPS-5 total severity (primary) and the SDS (key secondary, modified at the FDA's request: average of three items, work imputed as 10 if PTSD prevented work), both by blinded centralized independent raters by live video; exploratory measures in Table 7 (pp. 46-50); safety: treatment-emergent adverse events with relatedness determined programmatically as a twofold difference in frequency (p. 79), adverse events of special interest including terms for abuse pre-agreed with the FDA (p. 98), C-SSRS at screening, baseline and after dosing (p. 87), and blood pressure and heart rate before dosing, 1.5 to 2 hours after the first part and at the end of each session (p. 89). MPLONG: one CAPS-5 and SDS by an independent rater at a single visit 6 months to more than 2 years after the last session, health-economics data and a subset of safety data (p. 68).
outcomes.validity_norms: CAPS-5 described as the standard; a 10-point fall is taken as clinically meaningful (pp. 46-48). The SDS is called patient-rated on p. 48 but clinician-rated on pp. 20 and 46; it was administered by the independent raters.
outcomes.operationalization: Responder: a CAPS-5 fall of 10 points or more; loss of diagnosis: a fall of 10 points or more and not meeting criteria; remission: CAPS-5 of 11 or less and not meeting criteria (Table 5, p. 48). In MPLONG, 'durable' categories require meeting the definition both at the end of the parent study and at the follow-up visit (p. 74).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Primary and key secondary endpoints at alpha 0.0499 after 0.001 was spent on the interim analysis (p. 50); responder analyses and MPLONG comparisons carry nominal P values 'for descriptive purposes'; exploratory measures are classed as suggestive if nominal P was 0.05 or less in at least one trial (p. 134).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Blinded independent raters who never rated the same participant twice, with a separate database closed to sponsor and site staff; therapists were not involved in efficacy ratings (pp. 43-44) but recorded adverse events at integration sessions (p. 130). No blinding survey, participant or rater guesses, or expectancy measure is reported anywhere in the document (editors' search of the text layer and of OCR of the image pages). MAPP1 enrollees in MPLONG were unblinded.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary endpoint (de jure MMRM): MAPP1 least-squares mean change -24.5 vs -12.6, difference 11.86 (95% CI 6.32 to 17.41), P < 0.0001; MAPP2 -23.7 vs -14.8, difference 8.91 (4.12 to 13.70), P = 0.0004 (pp. 20-21, 55, 63). De facto: MAPP1 difference -12.04 (-17.46 to -6.62), P < 0.0001; MAPP2 -8.93 (-13.69 to -4.17), P = 0.0003; MAPP1 worst-case imputation P = 0.0293, base-case P < 0.0001 (pp. 131-132). SDS: MAPP1 difference 1.36 (0.25 to 2.46), P = 0.0167; MAPP2 1.20 (0.14 to 2.26), P = 0.0271 (pp. 58, 66). Week-18 responders among completers (nominal P): MAPP1 88.1% vs 62.2% (0.0152), loss of diagnosis 66.7% vs 32.4% (0.0049), remission 33.3% vs 5.4% (0.0051); MAPP2 86.5% vs 69.0% (0.0708), 71.2% vs 47.6% (0.0349), 46.2% vs 21.4% (0.0226) (pp. 21, 57, 65). Pooled subgroup estimates all favour MDMA (overall -9.7, -13.2 to -6.1) (p. 67). MPLONG: mean changes shown only in figures, nominal P < 0.0001; 'durable' loss of diagnosis 68% vs 33% and remission 39% vs 11% of those assessed (pp. 73-74).
analysis.covariates: Pooled subgroup estimates by age, sex, race, ethnicity, BMI, dissociative subtype, overnight stay and baseline severity, without interaction tests (Figure 21, p. 67).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The document is not a registered study; it gives no registration number for MPLONG or for the phase 3 trials.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not reported: the MAPP2 blinding survey or any measure of expectancy; the MPLONG data on interim psychotherapy, medicines and illicit MDMA use (collected, p. 68) and its health-economics data; numerical MPLONG means, differences or intervals; a worst-case sensitivity result for MAPP2; any result for the sponsor-developed health-care-use measure (UFEC, Table 7), which is missing from the exploratory summary (Table 32); and the values behind the exploratory classifications. Phase 2 efficacy is limited to 'the most relevant studies' (p. 138).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The clinical-study-report figures for the primary and key secondary endpoints agree with the published trials, and the de facto, worst-case and base-case analyses still favour MDMA. In the pooled phase 3 safety set, common transient effects (muscle tightness 59.6% vs 20.0%, decreased appetite 43.4% vs 10.5%, hyperhidrosis 28.3% vs 4.2%) were more frequent on MDMA, severe events were similar (9.1% vs 9.5%), serious events occurred only on placebo (0 vs 2), and peak systolic blood pressure reached 160 mmHg or more in 14 to 22 in 100 people on MDMA per session against 4 in 100 on placebo. The follow-up reports that the difference between arms seen at 18 weeks persisted among the 72% and 69% who were assessed, a median of about a year later, but MAPP1 enrollees knew their allocation, interim treatments are not reported, and the values appear only in figures.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The sponsor concludes that the two trials give substantial evidence of effectiveness in a representative population (p. 75), that MPLONG provides evidence of durability (pp. 22, 73-74), that MDMA-AT was generally safe and well tolerated (pp. 23, 99-101), that treatment-related suicidality was not observed and that MDMA as a pharmaceutical product has low potential for nonmedical use (p. 100), and that the benefits exceed the risks (p. 106). It attributes the treatment benefit to the subjective and prosocial effects of MDMA (p. 100), which, by its own account, the phase 3 programme did not measure (pp. 86, 98). It names functional unblinding as a design challenge (pp. 19, 43) but does not report the MAPP2 blinding survey, and it does not discuss how the follow-up's voluntary enrolment, the unblinding of MAPP1 participants or post-trial treatments bear on its durability conclusion.

timeline.event: Special Protocol Assessment: the FDA and the sponsor agree on two nearly identical phase 3 trials, run sequentially, and conditionally on a safety database of 200 to 300 exposed participants; Breakthrough Therapy Designation on phase 2 data (this document, pp. 17, 32).
MAPP1 published (90 adults with severe PTSD).
Burke & Blumberger argue that an inactive placebo cannot blind a psychedelic trial.
MAPP2 published (104 adults with moderate to severe PTSD), with an end-of-study blinding survey.
This briefing document and the FDA's own briefing document for the advisory committee meeting of 4 June 2024 (the FDA's was read by another reader).

On 10 August Psychopharmacology retracts three phase 2 analyses, giving undisclosed protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at the MP4 site as grounds; this document, written before, describes the MP-4 misconduct (p. 86) and does not cite the retracted analyses.

replication.where_it_stands: The sponsor's figures for the phase 3 endpoints agree with the published trials. Its long-term follow-up and pooled safety analyses are, in the sources read, available only in this advocacy document (and in the FDA's appraisal of the same data); no peer-reviewed report of the phase 3 follow-up has been read.

funding.funder: Lykos Therapeutics, the applicant; the document has no funding, authorship or conflict-of-interest statement. Its data are the sponsor's own clinical study reports and integrated summaries.
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated. The document is written by the applicant to support approval of its product.
funding.affiliations_note: The IND was opened by MAPS in 2001; from 2015 the studies were run through its subsidiary MAPS PBC; MAPS transferred the IND and NDA to MAPS PBC in 2023, and MAPS PBC was renamed Lykos Therapeutics in 2024 (p. 33).

what_would_settle_it: Independent analysis of the individual-participant data of MAPP1, MAPP2 and MPLONG, with the blinding survey, post-trial treatments, the timing of open-label crossover and illicit MDMA use; a follow-up planned from randomization, with blinded assessment at fixed times and complete ascertainment; and, for safety, a trial that records post-dose ECGs, laboratory tests and all subjective effects, positive ones included.

domains.note: The sponsor presents its own programme without stated criteria for what is shown: phase 2 results are limited to 'the most relevant studies' (p. 138), and the blinding survey, interim treatments and illicit-use data are left out.

No appraisal of the trials' limitations: functional unblinding is named only as a design challenge, the follow-up's voluntary enrolment, unblinding of MAPP1 participants and post-trial treatments are not weighed, and the published literature (about 1500 participants in non-sponsored trials, p. 32) is summarized without appraisal.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: All efficacy data and nearly all safety data are the sponsor's own; independent evidence enters only as literature summaries.

Tables are sourced to study reports and nominal P values are labelled; but conclusions such as evidence of durability, a benefit due to subjective effects that were not measured, and a low potential for nonmedical use go beyond the data shown.

domains.domain: Balance of the case for approval (the evidence against it, namely unblinding, the follow-up's limits and the effects not measured, is under-represented)
domains.note: An advocacy document by design; the counter-case is in the FDA's briefing for the same meeting.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a sponsor's briefing document (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used and the overall judgment follows the worst domains. The document can be cited, as the sponsor's report, for its study-report figures, for the existence and design of the follow-up and for its statements of what the programme did not collect, which are admissions against interest. It should not be cited as independent evidence of durability or of safety, because its follow-up results are interim, selected, partly unblinded and not given as numbers, and because nothing in it is peer-reviewed.

key_findings.finding: Sponsor's briefing document for the FDA Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee meeting of 4 June 2024, marked available for public release; Lykos Therapeutics, formerly MAPS PBC, seeks approval of midomafetamine capsules with a psychological intervention for PTSD.

Regulatory history: IND opened by MAPS in 2001; in 2017 a Special Protocol Assessment produced agreement on two nearly identical phase 3 trials conducted sequentially and, conditionally, on a safety database of 200 to 300 exposed participants; Breakthrough Therapy Designation (August 2017) on phase 2 data; final rolling NDA submission in December 2023; the FDA filed the application with Priority Review in February 2024; 10 meetings with the Agency since 2016.

Choice of control: placebo with identical psychotherapy, chosen with Agency consultation; to address functional unblinding, an active placebo (low-dose MDMA with therapy) and niacin were considered, discussed with the FDA and ruled out for their inability to address functional unblinding and/or a potential anti-therapeutic effect that could advantage the active arm.

Measures against bias from functional unblinding, agreed with the FDA: a blinded, centralized pool of independent raters (graduate training, at least 1 year with trauma-exposed people), blind to design, time point (except baseline) and site safety data, never rating the same participant twice, with interviews structured to avoid participants' treatment experiences; a separate rater database; therapists not involved in efficacy ratings; adherence ratings of therapy; an unblinded data monitoring committee. No blinding survey, guess data or expectancy measure is reported anywhere in the document.
key_findings.locator: 1.6.1, 3rd paragraph; 6.2.3 Study Blinding and Bias Minimization
key_findings.note: The absence is an editors' finding from searching the text layer and OCR of the 76 image pages for blind, expectan and guess.

key_findings.finding: Primary endpoint by clinical study report (de jure MMRM, mITT): MAPP1 least-squares mean change -24.5 on MDMA vs -12.6 on placebo, difference 11.86 (95% CI 6.32 to 17.41), P < 0.0001; MAPP2 -23.7 vs -14.8, difference 8.91 (4.12 to 13.70), P = 0.0004; figure N at week 18: 42 vs 37 and 52 vs 42.
key_findings.locator: 1.7.1 Primary Endpoint Results; Figures 4 and 5 (repeated as Figures 12 and 17, pp. 55, 63)

key_findings.finding: Week-18 responder analyses among those assessed, with nominal P values: MAPP1 (42 vs 37) response 88% vs 62% (P = 0.0152), loss of diagnosis 67% vs 32% (P = 0.0049), remission 33% vs 5% (P = 0.0051); MAPP2 (52 vs 42) response 87% vs 69% (P = 0.0708), loss of diagnosis 71% vs 48% (P = 0.0349), remission 46% vs 21% (P = 0.0226); the text gives 88.1% vs 62.2%, 66.7% vs 32.4% and 33.3% vs 5.4% for MAPP1.

Key secondary SDS: MAPP1 least-squares change -3.2 vs -1.8, difference -1.36 (95% CI -2.46 to -0.25), P = 0.0167; MAPP2 -3.3 vs -2.1, difference -1.20 (-2.26 to -0.14), P = 0.0271. SDS responders (a fall of 4 points or more): 38.1% vs 18.9% (MAPP1) and 53.8% vs 19.0% (MAPP2); 'In Remission' (a score of 3 or less): 42.9% vs 13.5% and 55.8% vs 40.5%.
key_findings.note: The MAPP1 P value differs from the published article's P = 0.0116 (the article's card); see the reporting issues for the SDS definitions.

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity analyses: MAPP1 de facto (n 42 vs 40 at week 18) change -24.55 (95% CI -28.30 to -20.80) vs -12.51 (-16.35 to -8.66), difference -12.04 (-17.46 to -6.62), P < 0.0001; worst-case imputation (missing MDMA values set to the worst MDMA value, missing placebo values to the best placebo value) P = 0.0293; base-case (missing values set to the placebo mean) P < 0.0001. MAPP2 de facto (52 vs 44) -23.72 (-26.97 to -20.47) vs -14.79 (-18.24 to -11.33), difference -8.93 (-13.69 to -4.17), P = 0.0003; no worst-case result is given for MAPP2.
key_findings.locator: 11.3 Additional Phase 3 Results; 11.3.1 and Table 30; 11.3.2 and Table 31

key_findings.finding: Pooled phase 3 subgroups (de jure; 94 vs 79 assessed): overall least-squares difference -9.7 (95% CI -13.2 to -6.1); every subgroup favoured MDMA, with wide intervals in small ones, e.g. age 50 or more -5.7 (-16.7 to 5.3; 21 vs 12), non-White -6.3 (-13.0 to -0.5; 21 vs 27) against White -12.7 (-17.1 to -8.3), no overnight stay -7.0 (-14.0 to 0.0), dissociative subtype -16.1 (-23.9 to -8.3); no interaction tests.

Exploratory measures, classed by nominal P (0.05 or less in at least one trial counts as suggestive): BDI-II, CAPS-5 subscales, TAS-20, SCS, EQ-5D-5L and one IASC subscale suggestive in both trials; three IASC subscales, EAT-26, HPQSF and IPF in one; DSP-I, CPGS, three IASC subscales, AUDIT, DUDIT and nicotine use inconclusive (P > 0.05 in both); no values are given.

MPLONG design: a multi-centre, non-interventional, observational long-term follow-up with no study drug or therapy; it opened after MAPP1's database had been locked and its participants unblinded, so MAPP1 enrollees knew their allocation, whereas MAPP2 enrollees stayed blinded until MAPP2's database lock and their own MPLONG completion; an independent rater collected CAPS-5 and SDS, with health-economics data and a subset of safety data (interim medical history, medicines, psychotherapy, illicit MDMA use, suicidality) at visits within one window.

MPLONG disposition: 60 of 90 MAPP1 participants (67%; 30 MDMA, 30 placebo) and 82 of 104 MAPP2 participants (79%; 45, 37) enrolled, 142 in all (75 and 67); declined or lost: 16 and 14 (MAPP1), 8 and 14 (MAPP2); 69 of 75 and 66 of 67 completed all assessments.

MPLONG participants (75 vs 67): time from the parent study to the follow-up visit mean 15.9 vs 15.8 months, median 12.7 (range 6.1 to 32.7) vs 12.7 (6.0 to 32.9); parent-study termination CAPS-5 15.9 (SD 12.55) vs 24.9 (12.31) and SDS 3.0 vs 4.3; male 42.7% vs 25.4%; prior sertraline 33.3% vs 16.4%.

MPLONG CAPS-5: in the effectiveness subset (all with a follow-up assessment; MAPP2 44 vs 37, both trials 71 vs 66) the sponsor reports that the difference between arms at the end of the parent study persisted to the follow-up visit, whatever the time since treatment (follow-up windows 6-12, 13-18, 19-24 and more than 24 months: 34/31, 10/11, 17/10 and 10/13 participants), nominal P < 0.0001 for descriptive purposes; the mean changes appear only as points in Figures 6, 23 and 24 and are not printed; source: MPLONG interim CSR.
key_findings.locator: 1.7.3 and Figure 6; 6.9.4, Figures 23 and 24; 6.9.5 (continued on p. 75)
key_findings.note: Values not extracted from the figures.

key_findings.finding: MPLONG 'durable' responders (meeting the definition at the end of the parent study and at follow-up), among those assessed: MAPP2, still blinded (44 vs 37): response 89% vs 57%, loss of diagnosis 75% vs 41%, remission 45% vs 16%; MAPP1 and MAPP2 (71 vs 66): 89% vs 59%, 68% vs 33%, 39% vs 11%; no intervals or tests.
key_findings.locator: 6.9.5; Figures 25 and 26 (percentages printed on the bars)

key_findings.finding: MAPPUSX, an ongoing open-label phase 3 extension (from 8 March 2021; interim cut-off 12 December 2022) for MAPP1 and MAPP2 participants who had received placebo (crossover) or could not be randomized or complete treatment: 41 treated and 30 completed, of whom 32 had been MAPP1 placebo participants, 1 a MAPP1 MDMA participant and 8 enrollment-confirmation failures; 2 stopped early for adverse events (a related recurrence of anxiety, an unrelated concussion).
key_findings.locator: 11.1; Table 29 (MAPPUSX row) and footnotes d to f

key_findings.finding: Pooled phase 3 safety set (99 on MDMA, 95 on placebo): treatment-emergent adverse events 99 (100.0%) vs 93 (97.9%); severe 9 (9.1%) vs 9 (9.5%); first occurring on the day of or 2 days after a session 98 (99.0%) vs 85 (89.5%); leading to discontinuation of study drug 1 (1.0%) vs 5 (5.3%); serious 0 vs 2 (2.1%); deaths 0; completed the studies 94.9% vs 84.2%.

Most common treatment-emergent adverse events (pooled phase 3): headache 71 (71.7%) vs 55 (57.9%); muscle tightness 59 (59.6%) vs 19 (20.0%); decreased appetite 43 (43.4%) vs 10 (10.5%); insomnia 39 (39.4%) vs 28 (29.5%); suicidal ideation 39 (39.4%) vs 42 (44.2%); nausea 38 (38.4%) vs 16 (16.8%); anxiety 30 (30.3%) vs 29 (30.5%); hyperhidrosis 28 (28.3%) vs 4 (4.2%); feeling cold 20 (20.2%) vs 6 (6.3%); restlessness 15 (15.2%) vs 2 (2.1%); bruxism 13 (13.1%) vs 2 (2.1%); mydriasis 13 (13.1%) vs 0; nystagmus 13 (13.1%) vs 1 (1.1%); blood pressure increased 7 (7.1%) vs 0; intrusive thoughts 6 (6.1%) vs 0; relatedness was determined programmatically as a twofold difference in frequency.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: subtracting MAPP2's published counts (31 vs 13 and 18 vs 3) leaves MAPP1 muscle tightness 28 vs 6 and hyperhidrosis 10 vs 1, as in MAPP1's registry record, not the 29 vs 5 and 9 vs 1 of MAPP1's supplementary table.

key_findings.finding: Resolution of related events (event level, pooled phase 3, MDMA arm): muscle tightness 119 events, 83.2% resolved within 2 days and 91.6% within 7; but intrusive thoughts 6 events, 1 (16.7%) resolved within 2 days and 2 (33.3%) within 7; flashback 10 events, 6 (60.0%) within 7; non-cardiac chest pain 6 events, 2 (33.3%) within 7; hypoaesthesia 9 events, 6 (66.7%) within 7; myalgia 12 events, 10 (83.3%) within 7.

Severe psychiatric events, 7 (7.1%) on MDMA vs 7 (7.4%) on placebo: on MDMA flashback (2), anger, emotional distress, obsessive rumination, depression, dissociation and grief reaction; on placebo anxiety (2), insomnia (2), depression, panic attack, suicide attempt, suicidal ideation and agitation.

Discontinuation for adverse events: MDMA 1 (severe depression); placebo 5 (mild suicidal ideation, moderate suicidal ideation, severe insomnia, abdominal pain, and one participant with a panic attack and two suicide attempts). Serious adverse events, all on placebo: severe suicidal ideation 10 days after the last session; suicide attempts 11 and 82 days after it (moderate, severe).

Programme-wide: serious adverse events in 12 participants of the six pooled phase 2 and 3 studies (10 given MDMA, 2 placebo) and in 8 of the non-pooled studies (all given MDMA); the most common were suicidal ideation (2 MDMA, 1 placebo) and suicide attempt (1, 1); of the MDMA suicidal-ideation events, one followed a low comparator dose and one began during long-term follow-up, 268 days after the last dose; the MDMA suicide attempt occurred 28 days after the last session. Two deaths, both in phase 2 more than 6 months after dosing (cancer-related), judged unrelated.
key_findings.locator: 7.5, paragraph after Table 25 (continued on p. 86); 7.6 Deaths

key_findings.finding: Misconduct: in the clinical development programme, one participant sustained serious harm from "significant boundary violations, unethical behavior, and sexual misconduct" in the phase 2 study MP-4; the event was reported to the sponsor after the study had concluded and was investigated, with no evidence of misconduct with other participants at the site. MP-4 (single site, Canada, 2014-2016; 6 participants in stage 1) is listed among the 17 studies supporting safety but not among the six pooled for the safety analyses.
key_findings.locator: 7.7.1.1 Summary (Neuropsychological and Physiological Effects), 1st paragraph; 11.1; Table 29 (MP-4 row)

key_findings.finding: What the phase 3 programme did not collect: subjective experiences of MDMA (sensation, perception, mood, cognition) unless reported as adverse events; any direct assessment of the prosocial or other subjective effects bearing on nonmedical use; desired, positive effects as abuse-related adverse events (throughout the programme). Abuse-related events of special interest (MedDRA terms including dependence, intentional product misuse, overdose and drug diversion) were pre-agreed with the FDA; none was reported.

ECGs were not collected after dosing in the phase 2 or phase 3 studies, and no thorough QT study was done; one ventricular arrhythmia occurred in the programme (phase 2: premature ventricular contractions, hospitalization for observation, metoprolol; probably related). No post-dose laboratory tests were done in phase 3, and most sponsor trials did not capture liver tests.

Suicidality (pooled phase 3, C-SSRS): lifetime ideation at screening 86.9% vs 88.4%, serious lifetime ideation 35.4% vs 36.8%, prior suicidal behaviour 27.3% vs 30.5%; suicidal ideation as an adverse event 39.4% vs 44.2%; intentional self-injury 3 (3.0%) vs 5 (5.3%); suicidal behaviour 0 vs 2 (2.1%); treatment-emergent serious ideation (score 4 or 5) 4.1% vs 3.2%, with one MDMA participant at a worst score of 5 and three at 4, and three placebo participants at 5 and one at 4; no one without prior suicidal behaviour developed it.
key_findings.locator: 7.7.1 Suicidality, 7.7.1.1 Summary; Table 26 and the three paragraphs after it

key_findings.finding: Blood pressure and heart rate (pooled phase 3): mean rise at mid-session in systolic pressure 12.8, 18.2 and 17.1 mmHg (sessions 1 to 3), diastolic 6.0, 7.0 and 6.0, heart rate 11.8, 17.0 and 20.4 beats per minute; by the end of the session blood pressure was near predose and heart rate still 9.2 to 11.9 higher. Peak systolic pressure (Table 27 is by dose level: the lower first-part dose, given to all 99 at the first session and to 2 and 3 participants at later sessions, then the higher dose at the second and third sessions, 94 and 92 participants) of 140 mmHg or more in 45.5%, 61.7% and 56.5% on MDMA vs 26.3% on placebo at any session; 160 or more in 14.1%, 21.3% and 21.7% vs 4.2%; 180 or more in 2, 3 and 1 participants vs 0; diastolic 110 or more in 1, 3 and 1 vs 1. Adverse events of blood pressure increased in 7 (5 mild, 2 moderate), none treated; one participant with a history of hypertension had 180 systolic and 110 diastolic or more at the termination visit about 2 months after the last session.
key_findings.locator: 7.7.2.1.1, 2nd paragraph; Table 27 and the text around it; 7.7.2.1.2

key_findings.finding: The sponsor's safety and benefit-risk conclusions: treatment benefit is likely due to the subjective and prosocial effects; treatment-related suicidality was not observed in the programme; MDMA as a pharmaceutical product has low potential for nonmedical use when taken as labelled; overall the benefits exceed the risks.
key_findings.locator: 7.8 Safety Conclusions, 4th to 6th paragraphs; 9 Benefit-Risk Conclusions

key_findings.finding: Proposed risk management: a REMS under which MDMA is dispensed and taken only in certain health-care settings once safe-use conditions are established, with monitoring during and after sessions and a patient registry; label warnings; a therapist training programme; single-dose packaging; DEA-compliant distribution; additional medication sessions to be studied after marketing.

Phase 2 durability: from MP-8, MP-12 and MP16 the sponsor infers significant durable improvement for at least 12 months for many participants; the long-term figures are within-group reductions from baseline in all treated participants, after open-label crossover, without a control group.
key_findings.locator: 6.9.5 (last paragraph); 11.4 Narrative Descriptions of Key Phase 2 Studies, 11.4.1 to 11.4.3

key_findings.finding: MAPP1 baseline by the amended clinical study report: earlier CBT 14 (30.4%) on MDMA vs 23 (52.3%) on placebo; EMDR 24 (52.2%) vs 14 (31.8%); prior sertraline 12 (26.1%) vs 11 (25.0%) and paroxetine 4 (8.7%) vs 4 (9.1%); mean age 43.6 (12.86) vs 38.2 (10.36); history of ADHD 15 (32.6%) vs 6 (13.6%) and of suicide attempt 16 (34.8%) vs 10 (22.7%); hyperlipidaemia 11 (23.9%) vs 2 (4.5%).
MAPP2 baseline ethnicity includes an 'Unknown' row: 0 on MDMA and 1 (2.0%) on placebo, with Hispanic or Latino 17 (32.1%) vs 11 (21.6%) and not Hispanic or Latino 36 (67.9%) vs 39 (76.5%).

reporting_issues.issue: MAPP1's baseline treatment history differs from the published article: earlier CBT 14 (30.4%) vs 23 (52.3%) here against 12 (26.1%) vs 22 (50.0%) in the article's Table 1, and prior sertraline and paroxetine 23 and 8 of 90 here against 17 and 6; mean age on MDMA 43.6 here against 43.5. The tables cite the amended clinical study report.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 51-52 (Tables 8 and 9); MAPP1 article Table 1 as extracted on its card
reporting_issues.consequence: Baseline history in MAPP1 is reported in two versions; the article's figures are the published ones, and the difference in earlier CBT (one of the imbalances noted on the MAPP1 card) is slightly smaller here.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that, by preferred term, 28.3% on MDMA and 18.2% on placebo in MAPP1 had a history of alcohol use disorder and 15.2% and 13.6% of substance use disorder, but Table 10, which lists terms of 10% or more in either group, gives alcohol use disorder in 6 (13.0%) and 3 (6.8%) and has no substance use disorder row.
reporting_issues.consequence: The history of alcohol and drug use disorders in MAPP1 cannot be taken from this document.

reporting_issues.issue: SDS responder definitions are inconsistent: Table 6 defines remission as responders with an average score below 3, but 'In Remission' is defined in the text as a score of 3 or less and exceeds the responder share (MAPP1 42.9% vs 38.1% responders; MAPP2 55.8% vs 53.8%); the MAPP1 text calls a response a 4-point increase; the SDS is called patient-rated on p. 48 and clinician-rated on pp. 20 and 46; the MAPP1 SDS P value is 0.0167 here and 0.0116 in the article.
reporting_issues.consequence: The SDS responder and remission figures should not be cited; the mean difference with its interval can be.

reporting_issues.issue: MAPP2 completion: the text says 43 placebo participants completed the study, while Figure 16 on the same page shows 42 (82%); the pooled Table 18 (80 completed = 37 + 43) and Table 29 (51 treated, 43 completed) follow 43.
reporting_issues.consequence: The same count as on the MAPP2 card (42 or 43 placebo completers); minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that, apart from myalgia, related events resolved within 2 days, but Table 22 shows that only 1 of 6 events of intrusive thoughts resolved within 2 days (2 within 7), 6 of 10 flashbacks and 2 of 6 events of non-cardiac chest pain within 7 days; the safety conclusions repeat that most events resolved within 2 days.
reporting_issues.consequence: Some psychiatric and somatic related events lasted longer than the text says; cite the table.

reporting_issues.issue: Treatment-emergent serious suicidal ideation is given as 4.1% on MDMA and 3.2% on placebo, without counts or denominators; the text then names four participants in each arm with a worst post-baseline score of 4 or 5 (MDMA: one with 5 and three with 4; placebo: three with 5 and one with 4), which over 99 and 95 would be 4.0% and 4.2%. The printed figures fit four of 98 and three of about 93 to 95, so one of the four placebo participants named is presumably not counted as treatment-emergent, which the document does not explain. Subtracting MAPP2's published two MDMA participants leaves two in MAPP1 (editors' calculation), whereas the MAPP1 article says serious ideation occurred almost entirely on placebo.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled comparison of serious ideation cannot be checked from this document; in MAPP1 serious ideation may not have been confined to placebo.

reporting_issues.issue: Reasons for early termination: Table 18 lists no COVID-19-related termination on MDMA and one on placebo, whereas MAPP1's supplementary Table 1 attributes two MDMA and two placebo terminations to COVID-19 closures; Figure 11 gives MAPP1's MDMA reasons as administrative, investigator decision, participant choice and withdrawal of consent.
reporting_issues.consequence: Reasons for leaving are classified differently in different sponsor documents; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: Blood-pressure increases are measured from each session's predose value in the MDMA arm but from the session-1 predose value in the placebo arm (Table 27, footnote).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'increase of 20 mmHg or more' rows are not strictly comparable between arms; the absolute thresholds are.

reporting_issues.issue: EQ-5D-5L is classed as suggestive in both trials although its MAPP2 P was 0.0557 (Table 32, footnote b); the sponsor-developed health-care-use measure (UFEC), listed in Table 7, is absent from Table 32.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exploratory summary is lenient and incomplete.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor inconsistencies: MAPP2 start given as September 2020 (Figure 2) and 10 December 2020 (Table 29); IND 063384 on p. 32 and 066384 on p. 33; cross-references to Figure 36 (p. 58) and Table 35 (p. 93) point to the wrong items; the MP-8 narrative contains a sentence describing a different study design (p. 139); MP16 enrolled 38 (p. 142) but Table 29 gives 33 treated; hypothyroidism is listed as allowed (p. 45) where MAPP2's supplementary methods list hyperthyroidism.
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial; they show that the document was not checked line by line.

reporting_issues.issue: MPLONG results are given only as figures and percentages of those assessed: no numerical means, differences or confidence intervals for the follow-up visit, nominal P values only, and the source is an interim study report.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of any persisting difference cannot be cited from this document.
